candidates.quote: In return the ruler acknowledges their praise by gifts or money which are often given publicly.
candidates.reason: Open-access full text of Finnegan's Oral Literature in Africa (OBP 2012 revised edition, CC BY); chapter 5 'Panegyric' is the standard comparative survey of African praise poetry.
candidates.supports: patronage and reward: the ruler's public gift or payment closes the praise performance; praise withheld or derogatory allusion used as a negative sanction (alt quote, count==1)
candidates.alt_quote: praisers can withhold praise or include implicit or explicit derogatory allusions as a kind of negative sanction
candidates.note: The OBP/OpenEdition chapter page (https://books.openedition.org/obp/1192?lang=en) served only a preview; the OBP chapter page returned HTTP 429 on three attempts. Full text obtained from the Internet Archive copy of the same OBP edition (CC BY).

candidates.quote: it is his duty to greet Lord with a royal praise name
candidates.reason: Peer-reviewed original article by the leading specialist on Xhosa oral poetry (Oral Tradition 3/3, open access).
candidates.supports: the praise singer's office: the imbongi's duty to greet the dignitary with a praise name, and the audience's expected repetition of it (praise performance order/audience)

candidates.quote: Obscurity in praise poetry could be deployed for political reasons.
candidates.reason: Peer-reviewed original article by Karin Barber (Oral Tradition 20/2, open access), the standard authority on Yoruba oriki.
candidates.supports: praise epithet as performance strategy: allusive, incomplete naming encodes discreet criticism of royal power (limits of flattery)

candidates.quote: The praise poem for kings and chiefs has also been adapted to serve the trade union movement
candidates.reason: Peer-reviewed original article on Ndebele/Zulu praise poetry (Oral Tradition 16/1, open access).
candidates.supports: the praise singer's office and audience: royal praise adapted to unions, election campaigns and public ceremonials

candidates.quote: directed at the Chief, decrying what was unworthy, praising what was worthy
candidates.reason: Peer-reviewed original article on the contemporary Xhosa imbongi (Oral Tradition 10/1, open access).
candidates.supports: praise performance: address to the chief, licensed criticism inside praise, and the political limits placed on it
